subject: bio
title: Cell Structure
subtitle: Eukaryotic and prokaryotic cells; organelle structure and function; microscopy.
concept: Cells are the fundamental units of life, bounded by a partially permeable membrane that controls exchange with the environment. Eukaryotic cells (animals, plants, fungi) possess a membrane-bound nucleus, whereas prokaryotic cells (bacteria) lack one — the circular DNA lies free in the cytoplasm.

Electron microscopes reveal the ultrastructure of cells. The transmission electron microscope (TEM) achieves a maximum resolution of 0.5 nm, far exceeding the 200 nm limit of a light microscope, because resolution is limited by half the wavelength of the radiation used.

Magnification = image size ÷ actual size. Resolution is the ability to distinguish two objects close together — increasing magnification beyond the resolution limit produces a blurred, enlarged image, not greater detail.

notes.heading: The Cell Surface Membrane
items: Found in ALL cells. Also called the plasma membrane — it is partially permeable and controls exchange between the cell and its environment.
Extremely thin (≈7 nm). Under the electron microscope it appears as two dark layers with a pale interior — the trilaminar (unit membrane) appearance.

notes.heading: The Nucleus
items: Largest organelle. Enclosed by the nuclear envelope — two membranes with the outer membrane continuous with the rough ER.
Nuclear pores penetrate the envelope and control the two-way exchange of materials (e.g. mRNA out; proteins in).
Chromatin = DNA + histone proteins (+ small amounts of RNA); it coils into chromosomes before division.
The nucleolus is a deeply-staining body within the nucleus that synthesises rRNA and assembles ribosome subunits.

notes.heading: Ribosomes, ER and Golgi
items: Ribosomes consist of a large and a small subunit made of rRNA and protein. Eukaryotes have 80S ribosomes; prokaryotes, mitochondria and chloroplasts have 70S ribosomes (Svedberg units = rate of sedimentation in ultracentrifuge).
Rough ER (RER) is studded with ribosomes — it is the site of synthesis and initial processing of secretory and membrane proteins.
Smooth ER (SER) has no ribosomes; it synthesises lipids and steroids and is a major Ca²⁺ store.

The Golgi apparatus is a stack of flattened cisternae. It modifies proteins (adds sugars → glycoproteins; adds lipids → glycolipids), packages them into Golgi vesicles, and dispatches them to their destination — including making lysosomes.

notes.heading: Lysosomes and Mitochondria
items: Lysosomes (0.1–0.5 μm) are membrane-bound sacs containing hydrolases at an acidic pH. They digest: old organelles (autophagy), engulfed pathogens (fused with endocytic vacuoles), and can cause autolysis of the entire cell.

Mitochondria (≈1 μm) have a double membrane. The inner membrane is folded into cristae, maximising the surface area for ATP synthesis. The fluid-filled matrix contains enzymes for the Krebs cycle, 70S ribosomes, and circular DNA — supporting the endosymbiont theory.

notes.heading: Cytoskeleton and Centrioles
items: Microtubules (25 nm diameter) are hollow tubes of α- and β-tubulin dimers; 13 protofilaments form each tube. They form the cytoskeleton (cell shape), the spindle (chromosome separation), and are the core of cilia/flagella.

Centrioles (200 × 500 nm) each contain 9 triplets of microtubules and lie in the centrosome just outside the nucleus. Found in animal cells (absent in most plant cells). The centrosome organises the spindle; centrioles produce basal bodies from which cilia and flagella grow.

Cilia have a '9+2' arrangement — 9 outer doublets + 2 central microtubules — with dynein arms that cause adjacent doublets to slide, producing the beating motion. Cilia move mucus; flagella propel single-celled organisms.

notes.heading: Plant-Specific Organelles
items: Chloroplasts (3–10 μm) are surrounded by a double envelope. Thylakoid membranes stack into grana — the site of the light-dependent reactions. The stroma (fluid matrix) contains enzymes for the light-independent (Calvin) cycle, starch grains, 70S ribosomes and circular DNA.
The central vacuole (surrounded by the tonoplast) maintains turgor, stores pigments and secondary metabolites, and can contain hydrolases (acting as a lysosome).

The primary cell wall is made of cellulose fibres (high tensile strength). A secondary wall may form next, with fibres in different directions for a stronger cross-ply structure. Lignin provides compressional strength. Plasmodesmata (cytoplasm-lined pores) link neighbouring cells through the wall.

notes.heading: Prokaryotic Cells (Bacteria)
items: 1–5 μm in diameter. No membrane-bound organelles. Circular DNA in the nucleoid region (no nuclear envelope).
Cell wall contains murein (a peptidoglycan) — prevents osmotic lysis. Some bacteria also have a polysaccharide capsule (definite structure) or slime layer (more diffuse) for protection.
Plasmids: small circular DNA molecules separate from the main chromosome; contain few genes (e.g. antibiotic resistance); replicate independently.
Flagellum: rigid, hollow, wave-shaped protein cylinder that rotates at its base — distinct from eukaryotic flagella. Pili: fine protein rods for attachment and conjugation (gene transfer).

notes.heading: Microscopy
items: Eyepiece graticule: a transparent scale in the eyepiece (usually 100 divisions) — must be calibrated using a stage micrometre (a slide with accurately known divisions of 0.1 mm and 0.01 mm).
TEM: beam passes through a thin section → images internal ultrastructure; max resolution 0.5 nm. Specimens must be in a vacuum and are dehydrated; heavy-metal stains improve contrast.
SEM: beam scans the surface → 3D surface images; max resolution 3–20 nm.
Limit of resolution = ½ × wavelength. Electrons have a much shorter wavelength than visible light (400–700 nm) → far greater resolution.

definitions.body: The ability to distinguish between two objects very close together. Limit of resolution = half the wavelength of the radiation used. A light microscope resolves to ~200 nm; a TEM to ~0.5 nm.
How many times larger an image is compared to the real object. Magnification = image size ÷ actual size.
The fine, detailed internal structure of a cell as revealed by the electron microscope.
A functionally and structurally distinct compartment within a eukaryotic cell, often bounded by one or two membranes.
Mitochondria and chloroplasts are descended from free-living bacteria that were engulfed by a larger host cell — evidenced by their 70S ribosomes, circular DNA, and double membranes.
Folds of the inner mitochondrial membrane that greatly increase the surface area available for ATP synthesis.
A dense region inside the nucleus that synthesises ribosomal RNA (rRNA) and assembles ribosome subunits.
Pores in plant cell walls lined with cell surface membrane that allow cytoplasmic continuity (symplast pathway) between neighbouring cells.

workedExamples.q: A cell is 25 μm in diameter. Its image in a micrograph measures 37.5 mm. Calculate the magnification.
Explain why increasing magnification beyond the resolution limit of a microscope does not improve the image.

steps.text: Resolution is limited by half the wavelength of radiation used. For a light microscope this is ~200 nm regardless of lens power.
Further magnification simply enlarges the same blurred image — two points closer than 200 nm cannot be resolved into two distinct points.
Electron microscopes use electrons (much shorter wavelength) → resolution of 0.5 nm for TEM.

mistakes: Confusing magnification (size of image relative to object) with resolution (ability to see detail) — resolution does NOT increase with magnification.
Stating that the mitochondrion has a single membrane — it has two (the outer membrane and the inner membrane with cristae).
Saying ribosomes are membrane-bound — ribosomes have NO membrane; they are free in the cytoplasm or attached to the RER.
Claiming prokaryotic cells have mitochondria — they have NO membrane-bound organelles.
Confusing the nucleolus (makes rRNA/ribosomes) with the nucleus (contains DNA/chromosomes).
tips: Magnification calculation: always convert image and actual size to the same unit before dividing. Express answer as ×1500, not just 1500.
TEM vs SEM: TEM sees INside (Transmission → through); SEM sees Surface (Scanning → surface).
70S ribosomes: found in prokaryotes, mitochondria and chloroplasts — useful for distinguishing these from eukaryotic cytoplasm (80S).
Endosymbiont evidence (for exam questions): 70S ribosomes, circular DNA, double membrane, similar size to bacteria, binary fission.

flashcards.q: What is the maximum resolution of a transmission electron microscope?
flashcards.a: ~0.5 nm (compared to ~200 nm for a light microscope).

flashcards.q: Why do mitochondria and chloroplasts have 70S ribosomes and circular DNA?
flashcards.a: Endosymbiont theory — they evolved from ancient bacteria engulfed by a host eukaryotic cell.

flashcards.q: What is the function of the nucleolus?
flashcards.a: Synthesises ribosomal RNA (rRNA) and assembles ribosome subunits.

flashcards.q: What is the '9+2' arrangement found in cilia?
flashcards.a: 9 peripheral microtubule doublets surrounding 2 central microtubules, with dynein arms enabling the sliding motion.

flashcards.q: What structural molecule forms the bacterial cell wall?
flashcards.a: Murein (a peptidoglycan) — prevents osmotic lysis when water enters by osmosis.
Magnification = image size ÷ actual size. Always use the same units for both measurements.

flashcards.q: How does the Golgi apparatus differ from the rough ER?
flashcards.a: The Golgi modifies, packages and dispatches proteins; the RER synthesises and initially processes them. Both are stacks of membrane sacs but the Golgi receives vesicles from the RER.

flashcards.q: What is the function of plasmodesmata?
flashcards.a: Cytoplasm-filled pores in plant cell walls that allow direct communication and transport between adjacent cells (the symplast pathway).

questions.q: Which ribosome type is found in prokaryotic cells, mitochondria and chloroplasts?
questions.exp: 70S ribosomes are found in prokaryotes and in the semi-autonomous organelles (mitochondria, chloroplasts) — consistent with the endosymbiont theory.

questions.q: What is the maximum resolution of a light microscope?
questions.exp: The resolution limit of a light microscope is ~200 nm, determined by half the wavelength of visible light (~400–700 nm).

questions.q: Which organelle modifies proteins by adding sugar chains to form glycoproteins?
questions.exp: The Golgi apparatus adds carbohydrate chains to proteins (→ glycoproteins) and lipids (→ glycolipids) before packaging them into vesicles.

questions.q: A micrograph shows a cell 45 mm wide; the actual cell is 15 μm. What is the magnification?
Which feature is present in prokaryotic cells but NOT eukaryotic cells?
questions.exp: Prokaryotes have 70S ribosomes (eukaryotes have 80S) AND circular DNA — both are distinctive prokaryotic features.
